nonblocking.claim_broken: The intake rule is that refusals made while a body may still be arriving close the socket. nonblocking.evidence: ASGI-measured headers: operator/put 403 {content-type only}, badhandle/put 404 {content-type only}, put-ct/video/x-msvideo 400 {content-type only}. By contrast 401/413 carry connection: close. The installed server is uvicorn h11 (httptools not installed). At h11_impl.py:262-264 it discards h11.Data after the response completes but keeps the connection, and data_received resets the keep-alive timer. So an authenticated caller refused before the read can keep streaming an arbitrarily long body into a discarded keep-alive connection past INTAKE_TIMEOUT_S. Inferred from reading uvicorn's code; not exercised over a socket (no network).

nonblocking.claim_broken: 'large_bodies ... must be the one the chat ingress uses, so both share the bound.' Under the ROUTERS convention register(app, rt), the ingress reads `rt.ingress.large_bodies` (ingress.py:119,197) and uploads reads `rt.large_bodies`. When the composition sets only IngressDeps.large_bodies, uploads silently builds a private LargeBodies(), which doubles the per-process large-body bound.
nonblocking.evidence: Attack A9: I set rt.ingress = support.deps(large_bodies=shared) with shared = LargeBodies(limit=1) and rt.media_store, called ingress.register(app, rt) and uploads.register(app, rt), then held the one shared slot. `ing.slots is shared` = True, yet the upload PUT answered 204 instead of 429. The two routes enforce different bounds. This is the brief's specified default and is covered by integration request (a), so it is not a defect in G4U itself.
nonblocking.minimal_fix: Fall back to the ingress's pool before minting a fresh one: `slots = large_bodies or getattr(rt, 'large_bodies', None) or getattr(getattr(rt, 'ingress', None), 'large_bodies', None) or intake.LargeBodies()`. Alternatively, raise RuntimeMisconfigured in pilot when no shared pool is found.

nonblocking.claim_broken: 'bounded bytes and time': the intake deadline covers only read_body. store.put_upload runs with no deadline while it holds the shared large-body slot.
nonblocking.evidence: Attack A4: with intake_timeout_s=0.3, I made put_upload sleep 1.0 s before storing. The PUT answered 204 after 1.01 s, so no deadline applied, and the slot stayed held for the whole call (in_flight returned to 0 afterwards). The store is in-process today, so the impact is limited. A real object-store adapter that hangs would pin one of the 2 per-process slots shared with chat.
nonblocking.minimal_fix: Wrap the store call as `async with asyncio.timeout(limits.intake_timeout_s): await store.put_upload(...)` and map TimeoutError to DeadlineExceeded. Alternatively, record in the evidence limits that the store call is unbounded and the slot is held across it.

nonblocking.claim_broken: The evidence (:60) and the case docstring say a large PUT with every slot taken is 429 'before its body is read'. That holds only when Content-Length is declared. A chunked body reads threshold+1 chunk before the 429.
nonblocking.evidence: Attack A5 used LargeBodies(limit=2, threshold=64) with two slow PUTs holding both slots (in_flight=2). A third PUT with content-length 500 got 429 capacity_exhausted, Retry-After 2, and read 0 bytes. A fourth, chunked PUT with no length got 429 after reading 90 bytes (threshold 64 + one 30-byte chunk). After both, in_flight was 0, peak 2, refused 2. This is intake.read_body's documented design, and the claim wording is too broad.
nonblocking.minimal_fix: Change the evidence and docstring to 'before its body is read when it declares its length; a chunked body is refused after at most threshold plus one chunk'. Optionally add the chunked variant as a case.

nonblocking.claim_broken: M3 limit 10: 'the route must stop reading at max_bytes + 1'. The route instead reads up to MAX_MEDIA_BYTES whatever the upload's own max_bytes is. This is a documented ponytail simplification that the brief marks optional.
nonblocking.evidence: Attack A12: an upload created with max_bytes=100 and max_media_bytes=8192 was sent an 8 KiB chunked body. The route read all 8192 bytes, then put_upload refused with 413. With default limits, a 100-byte upload buffers up to 64 MiB before the refusal, bounded by the slot.
nonblocking.minimal_fix: None required for this lane. The upgrade is the M request for a public per-upload cap on MediaUploads, then `max_bytes=min(cap, limits.max_media_bytes)`.

nonblocking.claim_broken: `destination_unguarded` and `completion_unguarded` claim the invariant 'the store's refusals leave as the envelope'. R83 requires that the named case fails for the invariant's reason.
nonblocking.evidence: Removing `@guarded` changes the handler signature, so FastAPI makes `request_id` a required query parameter and every call returns 422 `{"detail":[{"loc":["query","request_id"]...}]}`. The kill is on the first success assertion (`test_uploads.py:448 assert (422, 422) == (204, 204)`, and `:547 assert (422 == 400)`), before any store refusal is exercised. I tried an honest variant that keeps the request id but drops the translation (`guarded` rebuilt as a wrapper that calls `h(request, ids.new_request_id())` without catching). The same two cases kill it with typed DomainErrors: `infrx.contracts.errors.Conflict: state_conflict` from store.py:203 and `InvalidRequest` from uploads.py:180. So the invariant can be killed; only the listed edit is off-shape.
nonblocking.minimal_fix: Change the anchor to the guard's translation rather than its presence, for example replace `    guarded = intake.guard(new_request_id)\n` with a non-catching wrapper that still passes a minted request id, and keep the same cases. Alternatively declare in the list that these two edits die by the signature change.
